## Research findings: PRs #847, #845, #844, #839 (missingbulb/Claudinite)

**Review discussion note applying to all four**: none of the four PRs has any review comments, review threads, or formal reviews (all zero) — each was authored and merged by the same account (`missingbulb`) with no reviewer back-and-forth on the PR itself. The one exception is a single post-merge comment on #847. So "review discussion" signal for this batch lives in the PR bodies' self-narration and in the linked issues' comment threads, not in PR review comments.

---

### PR #847 — CI test time: prework timeout fix + suite concurrency
Fixed a timeout that never actually killed its target, plus doubled `node --test` concurrency.

- **Candidate lesson (strong):** `runPrework` spawned with `shell: true` and then called `child.kill('SIGKILL')` on the direct child — but that child is `/bin/sh -c …`, so the signal killed the shell while the actual worker process kept running (and kept mutating the repo) past its declared `prework_timeout`, with the scheduler reporting it as killed. Surfaced only because two tests with a 0.3s timeout took 10.05s — the exact lifetime of the "killed" child. Fix: `spawn(..., { detached: true })` + `process.kill(-child.pid, 'SIGKILL')` to hit the whole process group. **Rule suggested:** when spawning a shell command you intend to hard-kill, `shell: true` means a plain `child.kill()` only reaches the shell wrapper, not its descendants — kill the process group instead.
- **Weaker candidate:** owner's follow-up comment noted the local-box CI gain (106s→71s, ~33%) didn't reproduce on the real runner (only ~10%), because the "dead waiting" removed was serial time that a runner with spare cores was already overlapping. This is arguably just an instance of the corpus's existing "verify against a real run" principle, not a new rule.

### PR #845 — Fence-blind markdown scanning + line-count bounds vocabulary
Shipped 6 new declarative-check vocabulary keys and converted 4 imperative check modules to use them.

- **No new lesson found.** This PR is itself the *correction* — closing #843 — for an already-mined and already-corpus-captured lesson: an earlier round (not in our 4-PR set) added vocabulary keys without converting any checks, and the owner pushed back twice the same day ("So what are your action points about 1-4? No changes suggested?" then "you didn't convert any checks... I thought this was the whole point."). That exact lesson is already verbatim in `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md`'s last bullet ("A 'make it more general' or 'review this' ask is not delivered by the generality..."). Confirmed via issue #843's own provenance comment. Nothing further durable in this PR's diff.

### PR #844 — core phase 2: update task moves, `core-declared` goes blocking
Second phase of a two-phase pack migration (task relocation + severity bump), gated on a forced fleet pass confirming every member's declaration first.

- **Candidate lesson (moderate):** the PR's rehearsal fixtures all declared `basics` but not `core` — silently modeling a shape the fleet no longer had, "in the direction that hides a regression" (the `requires` closure still vendors the content, so the mount looks complete while the rule that would catch a missing declaration never runs). Fixed by prepending `core` to every fixture and adding one deliberate `core-undeclared` fixture to pin the legacy shape on purpose. **Rule suggested:** a rehearsal/test fixture's declared-pack list must track what real members actually declare — a stale fixture doesn't just under-test, it can make a real regression look identical to a healthy run. This is adjacent to (but not identical to) existing corpus entries about scan-based checks matching zero files; flagging as a possible new angle rather than a clear duplicate.
- **Weaker candidate:** the "fixture, not a migration record" argument for `consumer-safe-change` (a rule that is structurally incapable of firing on the old shape needs a fixture proving that, not a migration record with nothing to move) reads as a settled implementation rationale specific to this one check, not a generalizable rule — leaning toward "not a lesson."

### PR #839 — Declarative checks: review doc + five implementation bundles
Large, single-shot PR (review doc + vocabulary facilities + jwt conversion + perf + key merges + message discipline + barriers rephrase), done "at the owner's direction" in one pass, no rounds of rework visible in the PR itself.

- **No new lesson found.** No review pushback, no diff discussion, nothing recorded that changed course mid-PR. This is the PR that precedes the "converted no checks" misstep (which happened in later, un-reviewed-here work and is already captured, see #845 above) — but #839 itself is straightforward execution.

## Extraction results — 9 captured logs, 2026-08-15

Read all nine via `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>` (never checked out the branch). One genuine finding; the rest are clean or repeat already-documented territory.

### Finding — issue #801 (session `19223848-f245-5382-b02a-5653d99e5587`, files `1740Z`/`2235Z`/`2246Z`)

**Friction signal (misunderstanding / AskUserQuestion cost, #1 and #3):** the same session posted an `AskUserQuestion`, had it declined/interrupted by the owner, and **re-posted the identical question** on resume — twice, in two separate decisions:

- **Canon-flip endpoint choice**: asked `T00:16:44Z`, declined `T00:21:24Z` (4m40s); session paused, resumed, re-asked `T08:01:42Z`, declined `T08:06:18Z` (4m36s); asked a third time `T08:09:46Z`, answered `T08:11:19Z` (1m33s) — the answer taken was **"Flip, endpoint unset (Recommended)"**, the tool's own default.
- **"B6 route" question**: asked `T18:17:57Z`, declined `T18:22:04Z` (4m07s); re-asked verbatim `T19:07:28Z`, declined `T19:21:28Z` (14m00s); the owner then typed, in plain text, *"B6 seems not crucial for now. You can continue without it."* — a **third path that matched neither offered option**.

Total: ~29 minutes of session time across two decisions, both resolved by something other than a second identical popup — one by the tool's own recommended default, one by an answer outside the choice set entirely.

**Candidate durable rule:** After an `AskUserQuestion` is declined or interrupted without an answer, don't re-post the identical question on resume. Either take the tool's own "Recommended" option and state the assumption in prose while proceeding, or drop the closed choice set and ask once in open prose — a repeat identical popup still costs several minutes and, in both cases measured here, wasn't what actually resolved it.

**Provenance draft for issue #801** (≤200 words): During the tasks-dispatch queue migration (PR-1/Step-3 work), the session hit two decisions it needed the owner's input on — the canon endpoint config for the queue flip, and whether "B6" (GoogleCalendarEventCreator's hourly task) blocked Step 3. Each time, the first `AskUserQuestion` was declined/interrupted rather than answered, the session paused and later resumed with "Continue from where you left off," and the *same* question was posted again verbatim. The endpoint question needed a third ask before landing — on the tool's own "Recommended" default. The B6 question was never answered by either offered option at all; after the second decline, the owner simply typed "B6 seems not crucial for now. You can continue without it." Together the two round-trips cost roughly 29 minutes of session time. The pattern — re-asking an identical structured question after a decline, rather than defaulting and stating the assumption, or opening the question up — is what a next run should skip. *(Auxiliary, same session: `git stash` with no path, used to isolate a file for a red-first test, silently stashed the newly-added test too, producing a trivial "1 pass" instead of a real red; caught and corrected within seconds — worth a comment at the call site rather than a standing rule.)*

### Nothing durable

- **`2026-08-15T0002Z--issue-846`** — CI-runtime optimization session; well-executed (found and fixed a real `spawn(shell:true)` kill bug, corrected an inflated local-vs-CI speedup claim before merging). The only friction (a redundant background blind-sleep alongside a legitimate foreground poll that ran to its own 400s timeout) is the already-heavily-documented "blind sleep wearing a guard's costume" family — no new angle.
- **`2026-08-15T0337Z--issue-848`** — the `growth-extract` meta-task itself; this is the run that *produced* the existing corpus entries being read here. Clean, procedural, nothing to mine.
- **`2026-08-15T0423Z--issue-851`** — `tidy-issues` run; only friction was the `comment-classification` conformance check catching a missing "Comment class:" line — the check already enforces an existing basics rule, working as designed.
- **`2026-08-15T0431Z--issue-852`** — `growth-promote` run; clean subagent dispatch/converge, no waste.
- **`2026-08-15T1104Z--issue-856`** — file-placement advisory fix; the only correction (dropping a comment that restated its own declaration, and a test asserting a config value) is an instance of already-documented `basics`/`writing-tests` rules being enforced by review, not a new pattern.
- **`2026-08-15T2245Z--issue-867`** — the queue's first live agentic invocation; correctly triaged 23 issues via 23 small subagent dispatches (comparably fast to a single batched dispatch) despite inheriting the malformed double-`### Context` body from #801's bug — no confusion resulted, and the bug itself was already found and fixed in the #801 session.

Total: one finding, drafted for posting on issue #801; eight logs yield nothing durable.

*satisfiable* rather than for being the thing actually being waited on. Measured 2026-08-14 on the
  #768 session (`d585d2ae`): seven calls guarded by `[ -n "$(git ls-remote origin HEAD)" ]` — true on
  its first evaluation every time, and unrelated to the CI run, the canary cycle or the apply-stage
  session each call said it was waiting for — for **1342s (22.4 min) of pure idle**, on guessed
  durations (300, 202, 184, 181, 171, 151, 151). The same window carries the honest shape twice:
  `until curl … | grep -q '"status": "completed"'` against the run id (#846), and a real clock deadline
  (#843) — each returning when the thing happened rather than when a padded interval elapsed. So the
  guard must name the condition being waited on (a run's status, a file's arrival, a deadline) with no
  trailing padded `sleep`, or use `Monitor`, which exists for this. A guard you would not be willing to
  write as the *whole* test is the tell that you are sleeping and calling it polling.
- **`AskUserQuestion` blocks for minutes, so spend it on a fork you cannot take back — never on a
  confirmation.** Measured across 2026-08-14's captured sessions: **20 calls, 3640s (60.7 min)**, median
  ~170s, with the #807 session alone spending 1227s (20.5 min) inside five of them. The expensive ones
  were right to ask — forcing a fleet-wide pass, moving the update task between packs, which shape the
  #807 fix takes — because the owner does want an irreversible or fleet-touching step gated. The cheap
  ones cost exactly the same and bought nothing: 327s on *"should I watch PR #812 for CI failures and
  review comments?"*, 173s on whether the owner's own `caludinite-rules` was a typo, 64s on what a
  phrase in a file meant. Each was answerable from the instruction, the tree, or a reversible default —
  so answer it, act, and say what you assumed. Ask only where being wrong costs more than the ~3
  minutes the asking costs.
- **A "make it more general" or "review this" ask is not delivered by the generality or by the review —
  land the conversions it unlocks in the same change.** Twice in one day the owner had to say so:
  *"So what are your action points about 1-4? No changes suggested?"* on the #838 review, and then,
  after a round that added vocabulary keys and converted nothing, *"But you didn't convert any checks
  for 1 or 2. I thought this was the whole point."* (#843). The shape that satisfied him is the title
  #845 shipped under — *"Six declarative-vocabulary keys and the four conversions they unlock"* — and
  every key in that round and the two before it (#820, #825) names its first customer in the commit
  body. So a new capability ships with the caller that exercises it, and an analysis ships with the
  first of its recommendations applied: an unexercised key is unproven surface, and a findings document
  with no action points reads, correctly, as the work not having been done.

[{"sha":"a03810950f6b73077e46fd94c18d7248c9567c72","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/commit/a03810950f6b73077e46fd94c18d7248c9567c72","message":"The work-item queue: the whole mechanism, canon flipped

PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items
ready, and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the
precondition exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on
a no-go so "asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a
run-ledger watermark nobody can see.

The mechanism ships behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`, which only this repo sets
to "queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery, which stays in the tree until
the fleet flip deletes it. The two are disjoint by construction — separate issue
families, separate workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the
same config edit backwards.

- engine/scheduler/queue/: the item vocabulary, anchors, the tick's three jobs,
  the executor loop with its verified lease and post-claim re-verify, the
  janitor's four rules, the invocation call, and the create/wake levers.
- The claim arbiter is episode-scoped and ordered by comment id, the occurrence
  guard reads both created_at and closed_at, `after` compiles to a pick-time
  yield rather than a Blocked-by edge — each of these is a bug the simulator
  caught in the spec (F13, F15, F16, F18, S24) and each has a test naming it.
- Three additive task declarations: `after`, `on_interrupt`, and
  `invocation_endpoint` (a name, never a URL). The contract now also rejects a
  prework_timeout that reaches the executor's claim leash, which would livelock
  the item rather than merely duplicate a run.
- The signal collectors learn `[claudinite-work]` before any repo flips, so the
  queue's own churn never reads as repo activity to a precondition.

The endpoint map is deliberately unset: until it is configured, a hand-off
converges its item to triage naming exactly what is missing, which is the same
posture required_secrets has.

The design said "a CCR API call" and left the shape to implementation. The
routines documentation answers it, and the answer moves something: firing a
routine runs ITS stored prompt, and the `text` we send arrives wrapped in a block
explicitly labelled untrusted that a routine acts on only because its own prompt
says to.

So the payload names the item and the nonce and instructs nothing, and the
instructions live in a tracked file — queue/routine-prompt.md — pasted into the
routine. The issue-is-data posture survives the extra hop intact: behavior comes
from files under review, never from what an API caller sent.

Three corrections that a comment-shaped guess would have shipped wrong: the body
carries one freeform `text` field (structured JSON would arrive as a literal
string), the response names `claude_code_session_id`, and the endpoint is a dated
research preview whose beta header must ride every call — configurable per
endpoint, so rotating it is a config edit on one repo rather than an engine
release the fleet waits for.

Standing entry 11 is answered rather than left open: the endpoint offers no
idempotency key, so the agent-side lease is the mechanism that collapses a
timeout-retry duplicate, not a backstop to one.

Refs #801","author":{"name":"Claude","email":"noreply@anthropic.com","date":"2026-08-15T10:02:53Z"}},{"sha":"f0e18dcecd2af1fc2b57c4edad935a2a1aa043ff","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/commit/f0e18dcecd2af1fc2b57c4edad935a2a1aa043ff","message":"One call per item: the agent-side claim protocol deletes

Owner correction: the API should be called once per item. It is right, and it
removes a whole protocol rather than simplifying one.

The agent-side claim existed only because invocation was at-least-once — I
retried a call whose outcome I could not know, and a client-side timeout may
well have started a session, so two could arrive at one item and needed
arbitrating. But a retry is only safe when you know the first call did nothing,
and the timeout is exactly the case where you cannot. Declining to retry keeps
invocation at-most-once, and the lease has nothing left to collapse.

So the invoker calls once, with no `attempts` knob for anyone to raise, and
reports three outcomes instead of two. Refused (a status came back) is definite:
no session, a token or URL or routine is wrong, converge needs-human. Unanswered
is the one that matters: the item STAYS with the agent, saying so, and is settled
by a rule that already exists — a session that started converges it, one that
never did is swept by the janitor's agent leash. No re-queue that could
duplicate, no attempt counter, no bounded revert.

What survives is a check, not a claim: the session confirms the item's newest
hand-off nonce matches the fire it arrived on, and stops if it does not. One
comparison, and it still catches a replay.

The routine's stored prompt is now one line pointing at a tracked
instructions.md, so the whole of what a session does is under review — the same
rule the work item obeys. Canon's two endpoints and their token secrets are
configured.

[{"sha":"d9509ea7a5cb573c75432fafd6251244e3852d12","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/commit/d9509ea7a5cb573c75432fafd6251244e3852d12","message":"Replace an item body's section rather than appending a second one

Found on the queue's first live agentic hand-off. Every standing item is born
carrying a `### Context`, and the hand-off writes Context again — so the item
ended up with two sections of that name while `instructions.md` tells the
session to read "the issue's Context section", singular.

The two on that item were the tick's birth note ("born blocked until its first
anchor") and, second, the actual binding scope — the list of issues to triage.
So the section a session reads first is the one carrying no scope at all, and
the failure is silent whichever one it picks: read the first and it never
learns what it was scoped to, read the last and any birth-time constraint
disappears. It also grows, because a re-queue runs the hand-off again.

`withSection` now replaces a section of the same heading in place and appends
only a heading not yet present, so a body round-tripped any number of times
carries one of each. Replacing in place rather than at the bottom keeps the
body in the order a reader learned it.

`rollBody` had been hand-stripping its own `### Last verdict` before calling
`withSection` — the same bug, already worked around at one of the two call
sites. That strip is now redundant and comes out.

Fixes #879

ended up with two sections of that name while `instructions.md` tells the
session to read "the issue's Context section", singular.

The two on that item were the tick's birth note ("born blocked until its first
anchor") and, second, the actual binding scope — the list of issues to triage.
So the section a session reads first is the one carrying no scope at all, and
the failure is silent whichever one it picks: read the first and it never
learns what it was scoped to, read the last and any birth-time constraint
disappears. It also grows, because a re-queue runs the hand-off again.

`withSection` now replaces a section of the same heading in place and appends
only a heading not yet present, so a body round-tripped any number of times
carries one of each. Replacing in place rather than at the bottom keeps the
body in the order a reader learned it.

`rollBody` had been hand-stripping its own `### Last verdict` before calling
`withSection` — the same bug, already worked around at one of the two call
sites. That strip is now redundant and comes out.

Fixes #879

every key in that round and the two before it (#820, #825) names its first customer in the commit
  body. So a new capability ships with the caller that exercises it, and an analysis ships with the
  first of its recommendations applied: an unexercised key is unproven surface, and a findings document
  with no action points reads, correctly, as the work not having been done.
- **A retry across a call whose outcome you cannot observe needs no arbitration protocol at all —
  decline to retry and let an existing sweep close the gap.** The work-item queue's first invocation
  design treated the dispatch API as at-least-once and built an agent-side claim/lease specifically to
  arbitrate the duplicate a client-side timeout retry could produce. Owner correction (#854, commit
  `f0e18dc`, 2026-08-15): *"the API should be called once per item... a retry is only safe when you know
  the first call did nothing, and the timeout is exactly the case where you cannot."* Declining to retry
  made invocation at-most-once, and the claim/lease had nothing left to collapse — its outcomes reduced
  to "refused" (definite, converge to needs-human) and "unanswered" (the item stays with the agent; an
  already-existing janitor rule, the agent leash, sweeps the case where no session ever started). Before
  building dedup or arbitration machinery around an uncertain call outcome, check whether declining to
  retry removes the uncertainty instead of managing it.
- **A function meant to be safe to call repeatedly over an object's own lifecycle needs a round-trip
  test, not a per-call one.** `withSection` appended a same-named section instead of replacing it in
  place, so a work-item body that was written twice — once at birth, once at hand-off — carried two
  `### Context` sections, while `instructions.md` reads "the issue's Context section", singular: whichever
  section a session read first, the other's content silently vanished (#881, commit `d9509ea`,
  2026-08-15). Every existing unit test of `withSection` passed, because each called it once — and
  `rollBody` had already hand-stripped its own section before calling `withSection` at one of its two
  call sites, a workaround for the same bug nobody had generalized. Where a helper is meant to be
  reapplied across a hand-off, a re-queue, or a retry, write a test that calls it twice and asserts no
  duplication; a suite of single-call tests can stay green while the multi-call case silently corrupts
  state.
- **A check's `fix` text carries force independent of its declared `severity` — never write a
  config-acceptance escape into an advisory check's remedy.** `basics/file-placement` was
  `severity: 'advisory'` and never failed a run, but its `fix` text read *"or accept it in
  `.claudinite-checks.json` with a reason if it is a deliberate cross-cutting concern"* — sessions
  followed the words, not the severity field, and this repo alone accumulated eight acceptance entries,
  each a paragraph, for findings that were never blocking anything. Owner (#856, 2026-08-15): *"That is
  cost with no purchase. An acceptance entry exists to make a blocking violation reviewable; on an
  advisory finding it buys nothing and taxes every repo that hits the smell."* Fixed in #858 by dropping
  the acceptance suggestion and deleting all nine entries. When authoring a check's `fix` line, the
  remedies it names must match the severity actually enforced — an advisory finding's only remedies are
  act on it or leave it, never a config escape that implies a gate nothing enforces.
- **After an `AskUserQuestion` is declined or interrupted, don't re-post the identical question on
  resume — take the tool's own recommended default and state the assumption, or open the question up.**
  Measured on the #801 session (2026-08-15): the canon-flip endpoint question was asked, declined
  (4m40s), re-asked verbatim on resume, declined again (4m36s), then asked a third time before landing —
  on the tool's own "Recommended" option (1m33s). The "B6 route" question was asked, declined (4m07s),
  re-asked verbatim, declined again (14m00s) — and was never answered by either offered option at all;
  the owner instead typed past the popup, in plain prose, "B6 seems not crucial for now. You can continue
  without it." Both round-trips cost real minutes to a second identical popup that, in neither case, was
  what actually resolved things — the resolution was either the tool's own default or an answer outside
  the choice set. A decline is signal that the closed choice set is wrong, not that the same choices need
  asking again.

+  test, not a per-call one.** `withSection` appended a same-named section instead of replacing it in
+  place, so a work-item body that was written twice — once at birth, once at hand-off — carried two
+  `### Context` sections, while `instructions.md` reads "the issue's Context section", singular: whichever
+  section a session read first, the other's content silently vanished (#881, commit `d9509ea`,
+  2026-08-15). Every existing unit test of `withSection` passed, because each called it once — and
+  `rollBody` had already hand-stripped its own section before calling `withSection` at one of its two
+  call sites, a workaround for the same bug nobody had generalized. Where a helper is meant to be
+  reapplied across a hand-off, a re-queue, or a retry, write a test that calls it twice and asserts no
+  duplication; a suite of single-call tests can stay green while the multi-call case silently corrupts
+  state.

+  config-acceptance escape into an advisory check's remedy.** `basics/file-placement` was

+  each a paragraph, for findings that were never blocking anything. Owner (#856, 2026-08-15): *"That is

+  the acceptance suggestion and deleting all nine entries. When authoring a check's `fix` line, the

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

1	# Claudinite — the canon's own non-portable working rules
2	
3	This is the Claudinite home repo's own local pack: the capture surface for lessons that are
4	**specific to working on the canon itself** and would not make sense mounted into a consuming
5	project. Portable lessons — anything true for repos beyond this one — belong in the shared canon
6	under `packs/`/`skills/` instead (proposed by PR, or lifted by the promote stage).
7	
8	The growth lifecycle writes here automatically: the `growth-extract` daily task routes the canon's
9	own non-portable lessons — mined from repo activity and from captured conversations alike — into
10	this pack (each at the local promotion ladder's strongest mechanism — a check where the rule is deterministic, otherwise terse
11	prose below).
12	
13	## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate
14	
15	- **`canon-curation` lives in `.claudinite/local/packs/`, not `packs/`** (owner decision,
16	  2026-07-19). The canon home's curation duties are Claudinite-maintaining-Claudinite —
17	  project-specific content on the home's own capture surface. Do not propose moving it back, and
18	  do not describe the move as open or provisional.
19	- **Local-pack `run_daily` scheduling is ON — the fleet's default path** (same decision). The
20	  planner reads every member's local-pack daily descriptors by default; never reintroduce an
21	  "experimental / not enabled" framing or an opt-in seam for it.
22	- **Packs-tree segregation is barriers configuration only.** Any rule about what the `packs/`
23	  tree may reference is expressed by declaring/configuring the `barriers` pack (contributed
24	  edges, `siblings`/`scope` capabilities — extend barriers generically if a capability is
25	  missing). Never write standalone code that checks packs-tree segregation.
26	- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` records the mechanism only** (owner decision, 2026-07-23,
27	  #420). Status, phase tracking, in-flight-PR reconciliation and remaining work live in that
28	  initiative's tracking issue (task-prework → #394); a phased plan lives in the sibling
29	  `MIGRATION.md`. Don't reintroduce a status / open-questions / remaining-work section there.
30	- **Multi-session work hands off through the tracking issue, never a prepared prompt** (owner
31	  correction, 2026-07-23). The owner's opener is `continue work on #<n>`, so state not written
32	  into the issue is lost. Before ending a session on unfinished work, update the issue and let
33	  the session summary be a pointer to it — never compose a bespoke "pick up from here" prompt.
34	- **The canon never knows which repos consume it — fleet-wide aggregation is Sheepdog's domain**
35	  (owner correction, 2026-07-28, #520). Designing anything that spans repos, the tempting shape is
36	  a member list (or a "fleet" task) living in the canon. It doesn't go here: the canon carries only
37	  **mechanisms exercised on itself**, and the knowledge of *which* repos exist stays in the
38	  **Sheepdog** repo and its pack, which enumerates members at runtime from its own
39	  `.claudinite-checks.json` entry — exactly where the `fleet-roster` sweep already keeps
40	  it. So a cross-repo feature splits in two: a self-contained per-repo half in the canon, and the
41	  aggregation half as a Sheepdog fleet task. **No repo list exists anywhere in canon code** — and a
42	  derived fleet artifact lands in Sheepdog as a daily **auto-merged PR of a `GENERATED` file**,
43	  never a direct commit to its `main`.
44	- **A pack default stays in the pack — don't ask it at adoption, don't write it into a member's
45	  config** (owner ruling, 2026-07-28, #527/#528). An adoption question whose recommended answer is
46	  right for nearly everyone is "bad noise": it taxes every adopting repo to re-state the default,
47	  and materializing that answer into `.claudinite-checks.json` freezes a copy that then drifts from
48	  the pack and has to be migrated. Keep the default in the pack's own code, ask nothing, and let the
49	  rare project that wants to differ add the setting by hand. Read config as *optional* — an unset
50	  key means "the default", never "misconfigured" (`retention_days` unset is precisely why the
51	  growth-extract retention prune is skipped rather than failing).
52	
53	- **What Claudinite ships must run on the credentials and settings a member already has**
54	  (owner ruling, 2026-08-06). Requiring a member to flip a platform setting, or to provision a wider
55	  credential (a PAT, an app installation, a new secret), is a last resort — not because it is hard,
56	  but because it is per-repo manual work that reliably does not happen: the capability is then
57	  quietly dead in every repo nobody configured, indistinguishable from a Claudinite bug, while the
58	  automation's own report says nothing is wrong. Three members filed issues asking for the same
59	  Actions approval setting (ClaudiniteWebsite#95, EdFringeNow#205, TLDR#182); none was changed, and
60	  each repo's converge kept succeeding while its mount fell a day behind. Prefer the route that
61	  works with the Action's own `GITHUB_TOKEN` and stock configuration even when it is less direct,
62	  and where a platform behaviour blocks you, neutralise its *effect* rather than asking for the
63	  platform to be reconfigured. Where no such route exists — a capability the default credential
64	  cannot hold at all, which is why `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` is legitimate — take the requirement
65	  deliberately: name the exact scope, say why nothing weaker suffices, and have the automation
66	  report when it is missing rather than silently degrading.
67	
68	- **A change to what members receive is not verified until a member has received it — force that in
69	  the same session** (owner requirement, 2026-08-06: *"We're not waiting till tomorrow to see if
70	  something worked"*). Merging to canon is evidence about canon; the only thing that exercises a
71	  canon change end to end is a member's converge, and on a daily slot that is a day away — so a
72	  session that closes on "it reaches the fleet tonight" has shipped an unverified change and hands
73	  the owner a question they will ask anyway (asked five separate ways across 2026-08-05/06:
74	  *"Check status"*, *"Did the Sheepdog baselining work?"*, *"check now"*, *"How do you know 'the
75	  fleet is now fully on 076c029'?"*, and forced baselines appended to three consecutive `lgtm`s).
76	  After landing anything that alters what baselining delivers, drive Sheepdog's `fleet-baseline`
77	  workflow with `follow` and report what it did per member, unasked. Two corollaries. **A dispatch
78	  is not a result** — the API's 204 means queued. And **attaching a member repo to the session is a
79	  read you already have**, so attach the repos the verification needs rather than offering to: *"2
80	  of 11 members confirmed … say the word and I'll attach and verify"* bought a round-trip, one of
81	  four the owner spent that morning telling this session to attach repos.
82	
83	- **A code deprecation rides the standard `@deprecated` tag — never a bespoke conformance check**
84	  (owner ruling, 2026-08-09, #707). Retiring a field, option or module does not earn its own rule
85	  module, test file and catalog row: that is machinery to say what one JSDoc line says, and it grows
86	  once per retirement forever. `deprecated-session-scope` was authored as a `basics` check and deleted
87	  the same day it was reviewed (*"I don't think we want to add a check for every code deprecation"*).
88	  Put `@deprecated` on the **definition** — the one place the thing is declared, here the
89	  `session_scope` section of `engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs` — and have each sanctioned holdout
90	  pacify the warning with a comment at its own declaration site saying why it still carries the field.
91	  Keep the contract **validating** the lingering field either way: validation catches a typo that would
92	  otherwise strand a dispatch, and is not the same thing as a conformance rule.
93	
94	## Canon-specific gotchas
95	
96	- **Baselining backfill skips the home.** The nightly baselining that lands a `seededByDefault`

Comment class: other

**Provenance** — rule added: "don't re-post an identical `AskUserQuestion` after a decline" (`.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md`), captured 2026-08-15, session `19223848-f245-5382-b02a-5653d99e5587`.

During the tasks-dispatch queue migration (PR-1/Step-3 work on this issue), the session hit two decisions it needed the owner's input on — the canon endpoint config for the queue flip, and whether "B6" (GoogleCalendarEventCreator's hourly task) blocked Step 3. Each time, the first `AskUserQuestion` was declined/interrupted rather than answered, the session paused, and on resume it posted the *same* question again verbatim. The endpoint question needed a third ask before landing — on the tool's own "Recommended" default. The B6 question was never answered by either offered option at all; after the second decline, the owner simply typed "B6 seems not crucial for now. You can continue without it." Together the two round-trips cost roughly 29 minutes of session time. The pattern — re-asking an identical structured question after a decline, rather than defaulting and stating the assumption, or opening the question up — is what a next run should skip.
